title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Girl Among the Mill Wheels: Maggie's First Rebellion

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to read George Eliot's great novel of provincial life, family, and frustrated genius — closely, passionately, and in very good company.
The Mill on the Floss was published in 1860, and it remains one of the most emotionally searching novels in the English language.
At its heart is Maggie Tulliver — dark, brilliant, ungovernable — growing up beside a mill on a river that will, in the end, claim her.
Today's segment sets the world she inhabits — the Tulliver household, the muddy lanes of Basset, the comic and sometimes brutal machinery of money and family pride.
I'm joined today by three readers who bring very different eyes to this material, and I want to introduce them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has lent his voice to more classic novel recordings than anyone I know of.
He comes to fiction as a performer first — he hears the rhythms, catches the comic timing, and reads every character as if they're waiting to be given a voice.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don with a lifelong conviction that great novels are, above all, stories about individual character tested by circumstance.
He brings to Eliot a rare combination of moral seriousness and beautiful prose instinct — and, occasionally, a withering aside delivered with perfect courtesy.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class and power.
He will show us how the institutions of provincial England — the law, the family, money itself — operate as engines of exclusion, and how Eliot saw this more clearly than she perhaps knew.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because you've been assigned some of the most deliciously satirical passages in the novel's early chapters.
Thank you — and yes, I've been given some absolutely magnificent material.
George Eliot is doing something quite dazzling in these early chapters: she's building a world of comic catastrophe with the precision of a watchmaker.
Take Mr Tulliver — this wonderful, hapless man who is absolutely convinced of his own solidity in the world.
Eliot tells us exactly how this delusion is maintained, and it's a sentence worth savouring.

"He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance."
Pleasant jokes.
That's all it takes to sustain a man's self-image — a bit of flattery at the market and a glass of something warming.
And then Eliot adds — with perfect deadpan — that if it hadn't been for the half-yearly payments, he'd have quite forgotten the mortgage of two thousand pounds on his very desirable freehold.
What strikes me about that passage is not so much the comedy as the diagnosis.
Eliot is describing a specific failure of moral imagination — the inability to apprehend one's true position in the world.
Tulliver is not a villain; he is a man who has substituted the pleasant opinion of his neighbours for the harder discipline of self-knowledge.
And the consequences of that substitution will be paid not by him alone, but by everyone who depends upon him.
That is Eliot's great moral subject in this novel: the weight that one person's weakness of will places upon those nearest to them.
Edmund is right that this is about self-deception — but I'd want to ask what makes that self-deception structurally possible.
Tulliver's illusions don't float free — they are produced and sustained by the social world around him.
And look at what Eliot shows us when she zooms out from Tulliver to the parish of Basset itself.
"Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than half a curate, also poor."
That accumulation of 'poor' is not accidental.
Eliot is drawing a structural portrait — absent landlord, absent vicar, degraded infrastructure — the classic anatomy of a neglected agrarian parish.
Tulliver's private delusions exist inside a system that has already decided the fate of Basset and everyone in it.
And then Eliot gives us Dickison's public house — and this is where she becomes almost Hogarthian.
The description is exquisite: a large low room with a sanded floor, a cold scent of tobacco modified by undetected beer-dregs.
And Mr Dickison himself, leaning against the door-post — and here's the line I love —
"looking as irrelevant to the daylight as a last night's guttered candle."
As a performer, that image is a gift.
You can see him — the pimpled face, the melancholy posture, the total uselessness of the man in the afternoon light.
Eliot writes these minor figures with a painter's eye and a comedian's timing.
And this comic precision extends to the family dynamics too — and you've got a wonderful passage about Mr Tulliver's epistolary boldness.
Oliver, tell us about Mrs Glegg receiving that letter.
This is one of the great comic reversals in the novel — Tulliver at his most inadvertently magnificent.
Mrs Glegg has been sitting in the full warm glow of her own magnanimity, preparing to be gracious about the five hundred pounds she is owed.
And then Tulliver's letter arrives — informing her that she needn't trouble her mind about the money, it will be repaid within the month.
And then — this is the line that lands like a perfectly thrown dart —
"she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
He desired no favours.
The beautiful stupidity of it — the man is drowning, and he writes a letter of magnificent self-defeat.
I would resist the word 'stupidity,' though I appreciate the theatrical relish with which Oliver deploys it.
What Tulliver is expressing here is pride — and pride, even ruinous pride, commands a certain respect.
He refuses to be beholden to Mrs Glegg's condescension, and in that refusal there is something of a man's dignity reasserting itself.
Eliot does not entirely mock him here — the comedy is suffused with a kind of rueful sympathy.
There's something worth noting about who bears the cost of that pride, though.
When Tulliver writes that letter, he is spending not just his own dignity but his children's futures.
Maggie and Tom will pay the material price for every gesture of masculine honour their father indulges.
And Eliot makes sure we feel that — the comedy is always shadowed by consequence.
That shadow of consequence leads us to one of the novel's most vivid comic characters — Bob Jakin.
Oliver, you have a passage where Bob applies his extraordinary salesmanship to the formidable Mrs Glegg.
Bob Jakin is, to my mind, one of the great comic creations in Victorian fiction — and criminally underappreciated.
He is a packman, a street trader — and his technique with Mrs Glegg is a masterpiece of reverse psychology.
He holds up a piece of figured muslin and then immediately pretends to think better of showing it to her.
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
The dialect, the rhythm, the sheer cheek of it — this is writing for the voice.
And then he mentions the Princess Victoria might have worn this very muslin — and flings it behind him to spare her ladyship's eyes.
Mrs Glegg doesn't stand a chance.
What's fascinating about Bob is that he operates entirely outside the structures of respectability that strangle everyone else in this novel.
He has no capital, no family position — only wit and agility.
And yet he is, arguably, the most competent economic actor in the novel.
Eliot is showing us something important: that the people excluded from formal commerce are often more resourceful than those inside it.
I'd grant Bob his resourcefulness — but I think what Eliot values in him is something less sociological.
Bob is loyal — genuinely, selflessly loyal to Maggie and to Tom.
His comic vitality is in the service of a moral quality — the capacity for devotion across class lines.
That is what makes him more than a grotesque; he earns his place in the story through character, not circumstance.
And devotion, as we'll see, takes many forms in this novel — including Tom's long, disciplined, quietly heroic accumulation of money to repay the family's debts.
Oliver, you have that extraordinary moment when Tom finally delivers his news to his father.
This is one of the passages where the comedy and the tenderness become almost inseparable.
Tom has been working, trading quietly, carrying this secret — and then he tells his father what he has done.
"A good while ago, my uncle Glegg lent me a little money to trade with, and that has answered.
I have three hundred and twenty pounds in the bank."
Three hundred and twenty pounds.
Eliot gives Tom almost no rhetorical decoration — just the plainest statement of fact.
And it lands with more weight than any speech could.
Tom is a character who divides readers — he is not warm, not imaginative, not generous toward Maggie.
But this moment reveals what is genuinely admirable in him: a sense of duty pursued without complaint and without credit.
He has done a hard thing quietly, in order to restore what his father lost.
Eliot never lets us settle into easy judgements about Tom — and that refusal is one of her greatest gifts as a novelist.
I think the context of that three hundred and twenty pounds matters enormously.
It was uncle Glegg's capital that made Tom's trading possible — not Tom's merit alone, but access to credit.
The Tullivers fall because they are on the wrong side of capital; Tom recovers because he gets a foothold, however small, on the right side.
Eliot understands this mechanism with great precision, even when she frames it in terms of personal virtue.
What I find so remarkable about all these passages is how Eliot holds the comic and the tragic in the same hand — the same sentence, sometimes.
The laughter never quite drowns out what's at stake.
We've set the world — the muddy lanes, the market-day flattery, the Glegg money, Bob Jakin's magnificent cheek.
In our next segment, we'll turn to Maggie herself — the extraordinary girl at the centre of all this provincial machinery — and ask what the novel makes of her hunger for a larger life.

segments.title: The Weight of Patrimony: Mr Tulliver's Catastrophe

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into one of the novel's most quietly devastating engines: the ruin of Mr Tulliver.
A proud man, a stubborn man, a man who wills himself toward catastrophe — and yet, as George Eliot insists, not entirely to blame.
With me today are three guests who bring very different eyes to this story.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive, and he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score — rhythm, timing, wit.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose instinct is always to ask what a novel tells us about character — about the individual soul tested by circumstance.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as a forensic record of class and power — who gains, who loses, and why.
The question before us: how does a man destroy himself — and to what degree is destruction thrust upon him?
What strikes me first, every time, is the sheer audacity of that Oedipus comparison.
George Eliot invokes Greek tragedy — proper, classical, high-culture tragedy — and applies it to a Lincolnshire miller who can't find a lender.
The comedy and the pathos arrive in the same breath.
She writes, and I want to read this very carefully:
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
Now that is a sentence written to be heard aloud.
The double repetition of Œdipus — that slight insistence — and then "inflicted on him rather than committed by him": the passive construction carries all the weight.
Tulliver becomes a grammatical victim before he is a financial one.
Oliver is quite right about the sentence — it is brilliantly managed.
But I want to push on the moral question the comparison raises.
Oedipus, in the classical reading, is undone by fate, yes — but also by his own passionate certainty that he is right.
And the same is entirely true of Tulliver.
George Eliot tells us plainly that his will was not feeble — the text says so — but that external fact was stronger.
Now, external fact is stronger for all of us, at all times.
What distinguishes a man of character is whether he bends gracefully to necessity or breaks against it in pride.
Tulliver breaks — and one feels the tragedy is inseparable from that stubbornness, which is also his dignity.
I think we need to be precise about what "external fact" actually means here.
It is not fate in any cosmic sense.
It is the market for credit — and the market for credit runs through Wakem's office.
The man Tulliver most despises controls the only available capital.
That is not Greek tragedy — that is a very precise description of how provincial legal and financial power was concentrated in a single professional class.
And the narrator is doing something rather cunning with the Oedipus comparison — dressing a structural indictment in the clothing of myth.
The real tragedy is that Tulliver has no alternative lender — not that he has a tragic flaw.
Daniel, I take your point — and yet the novel gives us something equally wonderful from the other direction.
Because Tulliver's hatred of Wakem is not merely rational — it is operatic.
Listen to how she describes Wakem through Tulliver's eyes — this is pure comic characterisation:
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
That exclamation mark after "fellow" is doing so much work.
It gives you the exact pitch of Tulliver's indignation — spluttering but utterly sincere.
And the cucumber — that perfectly chosen, deflating English simile — says everything about how coolly powerful Wakem is, as seen through the eyes of a man burning with powerless rage.
And yet one must note that George Eliot does not endorse Tulliver's picture of Wakem as pure villain.
The narration is deliciously double-edged throughout that passage.
Wakem is attributed with every sin "to his certain knowledge" — which is the narrator's gentle signal that the certainty belongs entirely to Tulliver.
What we are watching is the paranoid logic of a proud man constructing a universe in which his own choices are someone else's fault.
That is a profound study in the psychology of self-justification — and a moral diagnosis, not merely a social one.
Edmund, I grant that the paranoia is real — but I'd ask where it comes from.
The text makes clear that Wakem has repeatedly appeared on the opposing side of Tulliver's legal disputes — the road, the dam, the irrigation.
Whether Wakem orchestrates these things or simply takes the cases that come to him — that is the novel's irresolution.
But what is structurally true is that the law serves those with the resources to retain the better advocate.
Tulliver himself suspects this — the narrator tells us he fears that Wakem has more law to show against him than Gore can show for him.
His hatred is irrational in its object but not irrational in its origin.
There is a domestic dimension to this catastrophe that I think we haven't yet touched — the role of Mrs Tulliver.
The narrator offers a remarkable little meditation on her influence — or rather, on the question of what constitutes influence at all.
Oh, the feather and the camel — one of the great comic set-pieces in the novel.
The narrator lays out this magnificent qualification — Mrs Tulliver's pleading has force, yes, but only because of all the other weight already on the camel's back.
The precise formulation is glorious:
"it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
"Credit or discredit" — that parenthetical even-handedness is so beautifully dry.
George Eliot is mocking the proverb itself, even as she uses it — asking whether the last straw gets too much of the blame and the earlier straws too little.
What I find most penetrating in that passage is the Dodson element.
Tulliver does not hear his wife as an individual — he hears her as the representative of a family he has spent his life refusing to be dominated by.
The narrator is utterly precise about this: his guiding principle, she tells us, was that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female Dodsons.
So his decision to go to law is partly a domestic power struggle conducted by other means.
He is not only fighting Wakem and Pivart — he is fighting the entire world that has ever made him feel insufficient.
And the debt this ruin produces does not disappear when Tulliver collapses.
It is transferred — to Tom, who becomes its instrument and its enforcer.
The passage assigned to me is Tom's confrontation with Maggie — and I think it is one of the most chilling scenes in the novel, precisely because Tom is not a villain.
He is a man who has sacrificed his own desires in the name of family honour — and he expects the same sacrifice from his sister.
He says to her — and one must hear the self-righteousness of genuine suffering in this:
"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you."

And then: "while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both."
"Respectability" — that word carries the entire weight of everything the Tulliver ruin has cost, and everything Tom has paid to reclaim it.
And Maggie is being asked to pay a different price — her inner life, her relationships, her very self — for a debt she did not incur.
That line — "there is no consistency in you" — is so brutal because it mistakes Maggie's richness for weakness.
Everything that makes her a magnificent human being looks, from Tom's angle, like unreliability.
And yet — and this is George Eliot's compassion — we understand Tom too.
He has paid in the currency he knows: labour, self-denial, ledgers cleared.
Maggie pays in a currency he cannot read — conscience, renunciation, the anguish of someone who feels everything at once.
And Maggie's own articulation of what she owes — her sense of duty — is, I think, one of the most finely drawn passages in the entire novel.
She does not merely submit to obligation — she constructs a moral philosophy from her own pain.
She says — and this deserves to be heard:
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves."
"They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us."
That is not submission — that is a fully reasoned ethical position, arrived at through suffering.
Whatever one thinks of its adequacy as moral philosophy, one cannot deny its seriousness.
I am moved by that passage — genuinely.
But I want to name what Maggie is being asked to renounce on behalf of — not an abstract ethics, but a specific social formation.
The "reliance others have placed in us" is Lucy's reliance, Philip's reliance — real human claims.
But the community that punishes her — St Ogg's — operates by entirely different logic: not love, but reputation.
Even Dr Kenn — the man of conscience — eventually recognises the impossibility.
The narrator tells us: "her conscience must not be tampered with; the principle on which she had acted was a safer guide than any balancing of consequences."
And yet the society around her will not honour that conscience — it will only read the scandal.
The ruin that begins with Mr Tulliver's debt does not end with the debt's repayment — it ripples outward until it swallows Maggie entirely.
That image — debt rippling outward until it swallows Maggie — is a powerful place to pause.

We've followed the catastrophe from Mr Tulliver's fateful borrowing, through his hatred of Wakem, to Tom's merciless accounting, and finally to Maggie's own extraordinary articulation of what faithfulness costs.
In our next segment, we'll look at what George Eliot does with memory and childhood — the mill itself, the river, and the world Maggie cannot return to but cannot leave behind.

segments.title: Blood and Belonging: The Fracture Between Siblings

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been circling the novel's heart — and today we arrive at its most intimate wound.
The bond between Maggie and Tom Tulliver — and the fractures that run through it from the very beginning.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels than perhaps any living actor, and he hears this sibling relationship in ways most readers simply miss.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the classical critic's eye — he'll ask us to weigh character against circumstance, without flinching.
And Daniel Rosen reminds us that childhood cruelty doesn't happen in a vacuum — it's shaped by the structures children inherit.
Oliver — let's begin with Maggie and Lucy, and that extraordinary moment when jealousy transforms Maggie's tenderness into something uglier.
What I love about Eliot — and this passage captures it precisely — is that she never sentimentalises the child.
Maggie Tulliver is eight years old and already capable of a very specific, premeditated cruelty.
And what makes it so devastating is that Eliot shows us the exact mechanism by which affection curdles.
Listen to how she sets it up.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
A little white mouse — that's the simile of a child who genuinely loves small, fragile, pretty things.
And then Tom looks at Lucy, and the white mouse becomes a target.
It's not that Maggie stops loving Lucy — it's that Tom's attention has made Lucy into a rival.
And Eliot catches that transformation with a comic precision that's almost brutal.
Oliver is right to call it precise — but I'd go further and call it morally exact.
What Eliot is anatomising here is not mere childish caprice.
It is the same weakness of will that will pursue Maggie into adulthood — the tendency for her affections to be entirely governed by how she is regarded.
She cannot sustain a feeling independently of Tom's approval.
And that, I would argue, is the seed of her tragedy — planted here, in a childhood quarrel about a little cousin.
The novel is extraordinarily consistent in tracing this particular weakness forward through time.
I don't want to dismiss Edmund's reading — but I think there's a structural dimension that needs naming here.
Maggie's dependency on Tom's approval isn't simply a personal failing — it's what the world has taught her to need.
Tom's regard is the only currency Maggie has access to.
She's been denied the education, the independence, the social standing that might give her a selfhood that doesn't require his validation.
Eliot makes this devastatingly clear in the very next chapter, when Maggie resolves to run away.
The passage is written as comedy, but the logic is quite serious.
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
The fantasy of escape is, at its root, a fantasy of ceasing to be judged by Tom — and by the family he represents.
And what makes the gypsy episode so gloriously funny — and so painful — is that the fantasy collapses the moment it meets reality.
Eliot gives us this wonderful passage about Maggie's education — or rather, the extraordinary gaps in it.
"In travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
She knows the word 'polygamy,' she's deduced the meaning of 'poly' from first principles — but she has no idea gypsies aren't well stocked with groceries.
It's a perfect joke — and Eliot commits to it fully.
And then — and this is where Eliot goes somewhere darker — the terror sets in.
Maggie begins to think the gypsies mean to kill her.
"She had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
Gradual cooking — only Eliot.
It is a masterpiece of comic gothic — but what I find equally striking is the theological precision of the child's mind.
She wonders, Eliot tells us, whether if the Devil were present, he would know her thoughts.
That is not a child being silly — that is a child applying genuine theological reasoning to a crisis.
And it connects directly to what Tom does in his misery at Mr Stelling's — he prays.
There is a passage I find almost unbearably tender — when Tom, having broken down in his Latin for the fifth time, adds a private petition to his nightly prayers.
"And please to make me always remember my Latin."
The whole pride of Tom Tulliver — that hard, unyielding pride — reduced to a whispered plea.
One should not dismiss Tom Tulliver as a brute, however tempting the novel makes it.
Edmund's point about Tom is well taken — and I think the education passages are where the novel does some of its most radical work.
Tom is being crushed by a system — Stelling's curriculum — that was never designed for him.
Latin and Euclid are instruments of class reproduction — they signal gentlemanly status, not useful knowledge.
And Maggie — who is intellectually far better equipped for that kind of learning — is excluded from it entirely, because she is a girl.
Eliot makes this contrast visible in the chapter where Tom remembers Maggie's questions about the Roman Empire.

"He had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
It is Maggie's questions — her intellectual curiosity, her instinct for context — that opens the world for Tom.
And yet she is the one sent home, and he is the one at the table with Stelling.
And Tom knows it — at some level, when she's gone, he knows it.
Eliot says he missed her grievously — that is a word she chooses with great deliberateness.
Not that he missed her company, or her chatter — grievously.
He had really been brighter, Eliot tells us, and had got through his lessons better since she had been there.
The irony is almost too neat — the child barred from the schoolroom is the one who makes the schoolroom work.
That's Eliot performing as a novelist of genius — the argument carried entirely in the drama of two children.
What strikes me listening to all three of you is how Eliot refuses to let either sibling be simply victim or simply villain.
Tom prays in a whisper; Maggie fantasises about gradual cooking.
Both of them are bewildered children trying to navigate a world that fits neither of them.
In our next segment, we'll follow Maggie into the years of loss — when the mill itself falls, and childhood gives way to something far harsher.

segments.title: Class, Debt, and Drowning: The Social Machine Grinds On

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
In this segment we're turning to the social machinery of the novel — the codes of class, the weight of debt, the slow grinding of respectability.
George Eliot is doing something remarkable here: anatomising a whole provincial world through its textures of feeling — the linen, the funeral customs, the boyish pride.
Daniel Rosen is with us — cultural historian, reader of novels as instruments of social power — and this territory is very much his home ground.
Oliver Trevelyan brings his performer's ear to the prose — he'll hear things the rest of us miss.
And Sir Edmund Leigh reminds us that behind all the sociology, there are individual souls making choices — or failing to.
Daniel, let's begin with you — because Eliot gives us a passage that reads almost like anthropology: the Dodson code of life.
What is she actually doing there?
She's performing a dissection — and the blade is very sharp indeed.

Eliot takes this entire class formation — the Dodsons, their cousins the Tullivers — and shows us how their morality is not transcendent ethics but the crystallised self-interest of a particular social position.
She gives us the line that is practically a manifesto for the whole passage — let me read it:

Their religion was of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it — if heresy properly means choice — for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma.
That final word — asthma — is devastating in its comic precision.
Eliot is telling us that for the Dodsons, religion is simply inherited bodily, like a chronic condition — not chosen, not examined, just carried.
And that's the point: a class that cannot reflect on its own ideology is a class whose ideology is perfectly secure.
That last line of Daniel's deserves a round of applause — and so does Eliot's.
What strikes me as a reader — as a performer, really — is the comic architecture of that whole passage.
Eliot builds and builds — baptism, sacrament, proper pall-bearers, well-cured hams — and then lands on the will.
The movement from eternal salvation to inheritance law is entirely straight-faced, and that's precisely what makes it so funny.
But then she does something rather beautiful — she pivots and admits the code has genuine worth.
She writes — and I love this phrase — that society owes worthy qualities to mothers of the Dodson class, who made their butter and their frumenty well.
That's not sarcasm — not entirely.
Eliot holds the satire and the sympathy simultaneously, and very few writers can do that without flinching.
Oliver is quite right to notice the restraint in the satire — and I think it's the key to the whole passage.
Eliot never quite condemns the Dodsons, because she understands what Daniel calls their ideology is also their integrity.
The passage tells us that a Dodson's pride lay in the utter frustration of all desire to tax them with a breach of traditional duty or propriety.
That is not, as Daniel would have it, merely a mechanism of social reproduction — it is a form of honour.
Burke himself would have recognised it: the inherited obligations that bind a community across generations.
When Eliot writes that they would not let their kin want bread — but only require them to eat it with bitter herbs — she is describing a real and functional social bond.
Unsentimental, yes — cruel at the edges, perhaps — but not simply exploitation.
I take Edmund's point — and I'd take it further than he might like.
The Dodson code is genuine — Eliot insists on that — but genuineness doesn't evacuate power from the analysis.
The point is that this code functions as a perfect screen against solidarity with those outside the family circle.
When Tulliver's financial ruin comes, the Dodson aunts perform the correct rituals of concern — and do precisely nothing that costs them.
And then you get Mrs Tulliver over her linens — a scene that I find almost unbearable.
Listen to what she says over these pieces of cloth that are about to be sold:

To think o' these cloths as I spun myself, and Job Haxey wove 'em, and brought the piece home on his back, as I remember standing at the door and seeing him come, before I ever thought o' marrying your father!
This is a woman watching her own labour — her identity, her history — being turned into exchangeable commodities.
The particular stitch that nobody else could make, the pattern she chose, the marking — it's all about irreducible personhood being dissolved by the market.
The detail that always floors me — and I have read this passage aloud more than once — is: they must cut the cloth to get it out, for it's a particular stitch.
The only way to recover her mark on the world is to destroy what she made.
And then she turns to Tom — this blond, usually passive woman in a moment of extraordinary animation — and says:
You'll never have one of 'em, my boy, and I meant 'em for you.
The novel in a single sentence.
Everything intended, nothing inherited.
That phrase will stay with me.
Daniel, you've also brought us the passage about Tom and Philip — that cold, raking analysis of how boyhood enmity calcifies into adult cruelty.
How does that fit into the picture you're building?
The passage about Tom and Philip is where Eliot is at her most merciless — and I mean that as a compliment.
She gives us that great structural metaphor — boys welded together by transient feeling, but made of incompatible metals.
The narrator's exact words are:
If boys and men are to be welded together in the glow of transient feeling, they must be made of metal that will mix, else they inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out.
The heat is pity — a temporary warmth generated by shared suffering during Tom's illness.
And when it goes, what's left is class — old Tulliver's blood prejudice against Wakem, transmitted intact to Tom.
Mr Tulliver himself says it — the gray colt may chance to kick like his black sire.
The inheritance isn't property here — it's hatred, passed down as faithfully as the family silver.
I want to resist — gently — the idea that Tom is simply a vehicle for inherited class prejudice.
Eliot is more precise than that, and the precision is in the passage Daniel hasn't yet quoted — the one about Tom's moral self-deception.
She writes — with that characteristic clinical gentleness of hers —

Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them.
That is not class — that is a portrait of a particular kind of moral obtuseness that is entirely individual.
Tom is not wicked — he is incapable of the self-examination that might make him good.
Eliot is writing about the limits of a certain masculine character — and she is writing about it as tragedy.
Edmund is right that the portrait is individual — but the individual is always also the social, in Eliot.
What she shows us in that same passage is the mechanism: Tom has absorbed the family's enmity toward Wakem so completely that he mistakes it for principle.

She tells us he did not know how much of an old boyish repulsion and of mere personal pride and animosity was concerned in the bitter severity of the words by which he meant to do the duty of a son and a brother.
Duty — the Dodson-Tulliver word above all others — becomes the cover story for cruelty.
And it's Maggie who bears the cost — she writhed under the demonstrable truth of the character he had given to her conduct.
The word writhed — Eliot chooses it carefully.
It's a physical word for a spiritual torment — and it prepares us for everything Maggie endures in the later chapters.
Because in the Stephen Guest section we get the full account of that battle — and Eliot gives us one of the most remarkable sentences in the whole novel.
She's describing Maggie's struggle between her own longing and her loyalty — and she reaches for this image:
She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul.
Organs of her soul — what an extraordinary phrase.
Faith and sympathy aren't decorative virtues for Maggie — they are load-bearing, structural.
Remove them and she doesn't become freer — she becomes less herself.
That is the novel's moral centre, stated plainly.
And what's striking is that Eliot doesn't sentimentalise Maggie's renunciation — she is absolutely clear-eyed about what it costs her.
The narrator tells us there were moments in which a cruel selfishness seemed to be getting possession of her — and asks: why should not Lucy, why should not Philip, suffer?
Eliot grants Maggie the full force of the temptation — and then shows us why she cannot yield to it without self-annihilation.
This is not social critique — this is moral philosophy rendered as fiction of the highest order.
I won't quarrel with Edmund on Maggie — the moral analysis is superb.
But I want to ask what the novel has done to Maggie by this point — what the system has produced.
A brilliant woman, cramped at every turn — by Tom's authority, by the Dodson code, by the market that sold her mother's linens.
And now the best she can do is choose not to harm others — not to act, not to reach for what she wants.
Eliot calls that freedom — and it is a kind of freedom — but we should also name what it costs.
The social machine has narrowed Maggie's world until renunciation is the only heroism available to her.
That's a thought that will carry us forward — the heroism that the machine leaves room for.
We've moved from the Dodson linen cupboard to the very architecture of a soul — and that is exactly what The Mill on the Floss demands of its readers.
Thank you Daniel, Oliver, Edmund — we'll return after a short break to look at what the novel does with water, memory, and the impossible pull of home.

segments.title: The Wit of Resignation: Comedy in a Collapsing World

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're looking at something that makes this novel genuinely unusual among the great Victorian tragedies — its comedy.
Not comic relief in the cheap sense, but a wit so embedded in the novel's moral intelligence that it becomes inseparable from its sorrow.
To explore this, I'm delighted to have Oliver Trevelyan with us — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic audiobooks than any living person.
Oliver hears prose the way a musician hears a score — rhythm, timing, the exact moment a sentence turns.
Also with us, Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, reader of the novel as moral drama first and social document second.
Edmund brings a patience with the text that I find consistently illuminating.
And Dr Daniel Rosen — cultural historian, who reads every comic moment in a Victorian novel as also a political one.
Daniel, I suspect, will find that the laughter in this novel is never quite innocent.
Oliver — let's begin with you, because the passages we're looking at today feel tailor-made for a performer.
Where does Eliot's comedy live, for you, in these pages?
It lives in the sentence itself — that's the first thing to understand about Eliot's comedy.
It's not a matter of comic scenes or funny characters — it's the prose that has the timing.
Take the passage about Mrs Tulliver — thirteen years of marriage, thirteen years of saying exactly the wrong thing to her husband.
And then Eliot writes this:

"Some minds are wonderful for keeping their bloom in this way, as a patriarchal goldfish apparently retains to the last its youthful illusion that it can swim in a straight line beyond the encircling glass."
A patriarchal goldfish.
That word — patriarchal — is doing everything.
It's not just a goldfish bumping its nose against the glass — it's an ancient, dignified, self-important goldfish doing it.
And then the next sentence delivers the verdict with perfect composure:
"Mrs Tulliver was an amiable fish of this kind, and after running her head against the same resisting medium for thirteen years would go at it again to-day with undulled alacrity."
Undulled alacrity — that's the joke, and the tenderness, and the diagnosis, all in two words.
What strikes me about that passage is that the comedy doesn't diminish Mrs Tulliver — it defines her.
Her persistence is both absurd and, in its way, a form of faith.
She continues to believe in the possibility of persuading Mr Tulliver — that is not stupidity, it is a kind of conjugal loyalty that the world has failed to reward.
This is what I think Eliot's comedy does at its best — it holds character steady while the world around it shifts.
Dr Johnson observed that the business of the comic writer is to copy nature — and Eliot, here, is doing precisely that.
I'd want to push on that word 'loyalty,' Edmund, because I think what Eliot is also satirising here is the structural position of Mrs Tulliver.
She has no power in this marriage — no property, no legal standing, no effective voice.
The goldfish image is devastatingly precise in that regard — the glass is not arbitrary, it's the enclosure that defines her entire existence.
But where I find Eliot's comedy most politically sharp is in the St Ogg's passage — the one about what would have happened if Maggie had returned as Mrs Stephen Guest.
Eliot sets it up with a line that sounds almost like a shrug:
"We judge others according to results; how else?—not knowing the process by which results are arrived at."
That 'how else' is the whole ideology of St Ogg's society in two words.
It is a system that cannot imagine moral interiority — only outcomes, only respectability confirmed by success.
And then what Eliot does next is extraordinary — she lets St Ogg's speak in its own voice.
That long passage of reported gossip — it's a kind of ventriloquism, and devastating ventriloquism at that.
Listen to this — the town imagining what it would have said had Maggie married Stephen:

"and a deformed young man, you know!—and young Guest so very fascinating; and, they say, he positively worships her (to be sure, that can't last!), and he ran away with her in the boat quite against her will, and what could she do?"
That parenthesis — 'to be sure, that can't last' — is absolutely lethal.
Society absolves Maggie in the same breath that it insults Philip, gossips about Stephen's constancy, and worries about Miss Deane's feelings.
The comedy is indistinguishable from the cruelty — which is precisely the point.
One must note, though, that the comedy of the St Ogg's passage only lands because Eliot has already established the moral stakes.
We know what Maggie actually sacrificed — what she actually endured — which is why the town's breezy rationalisation is so appalling.
And I think that same structure — comedy that costs something — is at work in the childhood passages Oliver hasn't yet touched on.
That extraordinary passage defending the reality of Maggie's childhood anguish — it begins in apparent comedy and arrives somewhere quite painful.
You're right, Edmund — and the passage with Tom in disguise is the comic peak before that shift.
Tom has spent — one must imagine — considerable time in front of the looking-glass, trying to look fierce.
His fundamental problem is that he has, and I quote:
"a pair of amiable blue-gray eyes and round pink cheeks that refused to look formidable, let him frown as he would before the looking-glass."
Cheeks that refused to look formidable — they have their own agency, these cheeks.
So his solution: burnt cork eyebrows that met in what the narrator calls, with perfect solemnity, 'a satisfactory manner over his nose.'
But what I love most is this detail about the frowning practice:
"Philip had once told him of a man who had a horseshoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning might to make a horseshoe on his forehead."
All his frowning might — it's irresistible, and it's also rather touching, because this is Tom trying to become something his nature won't allow.
And that detail about Philip — it's Philip who tells Tom about the horseshoe frown — is quietly significant.
Philip is the imaginative one, the one who knows things, who reads — and Tom uses that knowledge to perform aggression.
That dynamic — Philip's inner life instrumentalised for Tom's theatre of dominance — is the whole novel in miniature.
But what Edmund raised about the childhood anguish passage matters enormously here too.
Eliot is doing something philosophically serious when she defends Maggie's grief as equal in intensity to adult suffering.
She writes:

"Very trivial, perhaps, this anguish seems to weather-worn mortals who have to think of Christmas bills, dead loves, and broken friendships; but it was not less bitter to Maggie—perhaps it was even more bitter—than what we are fond of calling antithetically the real troubles of mature life."
That word 'antithetically' is a rebuke to every adult who has dismissed a child's pain with the promise of future suffering.
And the class dimension is sharp — it's 'weather-worn mortals' who condescend, people whose experience has calcified into common sense.
I read that passage differently from Daniel, as I suspect he expects.
I don't think Eliot's target is a class — it's a failure of sympathy that is entirely universal.
The passage is about the irreversibility of experience — the fact that once the texture of childhood has blended into adult life, you cannot retrieve the original consciousness.
And there is a philosophical humility there — Eliot is not claiming to have recovered it, only pleading that we should not pooh-pooh the griefs of our children.
The comedy has done its work by then — established Maggie as ludicrous, helpless, sitting among her black locks.
And then the narrator turns and says: but this is not trivial.
And the Ajax comparison just before that turn is wonderful — 'She sat as helpless and despairing among her black locks as Ajax among the slaughtered sheep.'
A little girl who's cut off her hair, compared to a Greek hero maddened by the gods — it's absurd, it's funny, and it's completely right.
Because to Maggie, in that moment, it is an epic catastrophe.
And Eliot uses the comedy to carry us into the catastrophe rather than away from it.
That, to me, is the genius of her as a novelist — the joke is the beginning of the sympathy, not the alternative to it.
The joke as the beginning of sympathy — that's a beautiful way to put it, Oliver.
And I think what this conversation has shown is that Eliot's comedy is never decorative — it's load-bearing.
From Mrs Tulliver's goldfish persistence, to Tom's horseshoe frown, to St Ogg's conveniently forgiving morality — the wit is always doing the novel's most essential work.
We'll be back after the break to look more closely at how character is tested when the world begins, in earnest, to collapse around Maggie Tulliver.

segments.title: Character Forged in Sorrow: Maggie's Hunger Transforms

utterances.text: We turn now to what is, for many readers, the beating heart of this novel — the formation of Maggie Tulliver's character under pressure.
Not the grand Maggie of the later books, but the child — passionate, hungry, misunderstood — being shaped, passage by passage, into someone capable of tragedy.

Sir Edmund Leigh has been wrestling with this arc across six passages, and I want to begin with him — because he sees something in Maggie's moral development that I think will sharpen everything that follows.
Thank you.
What strikes me most forcefully about this sequence of passages is that George Eliot is doing something almost Aristotelian.
She is tracking the gap — the tragic gap — between the magnitude of the passion and the smallness of the available action.
She even reaches for the Greek.

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action."
That Greek phrase — τι μέγεθος — the certain greatness, the requisite magnitude — Eliot deploys it with complete confidence, and earns it.
The passion is real and the action is — Lucy, pushed into mud.
And Eliot names her — "poor little pink-and-white Lucy" — which is doing so much comic and moral work simultaneously.
Pink-and-white is not just a colour — it's a whole social type.
Maggie is brown and fierce and doesn't fit.
Lucy is the world's idea of what a little girl should be, and the world is about to receive her, muddy, from the cow-trodden ground.
But what I hear in that passage — as a performer — is that Eliot is laughing and grieving at precisely the same moment.
That is a very difficult thing to do on the page, and she makes it look effortless.
There is something else that Lucy represents in that scene, though.
She is the child who fits — the child the world rewards with tenderness and approval.
And Eliot is precise about what Maggie is reaching for when she pushes her.
The narrator tells us — and this is almost unbearable in its honesty — that Maggie had "fashioned the world afresh in her own thoughts," expecting love and tenderness, and found only fault-finding.
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
The soul made up of wants — and nothing, no institution, no family, no community, is equipped to meet those wants.
That is not a personal failing of Maggie's — that is an indictment.
I would resist the word indictment — though I take Daniel's point seriously.
Eliot's observation is more tender than that — and more honest about the limits of what any world can offer.
The narrator says "we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present."
That "we" is doing something important — Eliot is implicating the reader, not just society.
Our tendency to discount early suffering because we can see the larger shape of a life — Eliot refuses that comfort.
She insists that the child's present pain is real and complete in itself.
And when that pain touches the father — when Maggie sees Mr Tulliver helpless — something shifts in the register entirely.
Eliot reaches for a phrase that I find almost impossibly moving to read aloud.
"that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish."
Primitive — not as an insult, but as the deepest possible compliment.
This is the love that precedes language, precedes argument, precedes the whole machinery of Victorian moral reasoning.
And it falls on a child who is also — Eliot says — experiencing one of those supreme moments when everything else falls away as insignificant.
"Poor child" — just those two words before the passage — Eliot earns them completely.
And yet that primitive love is also what the novel uses to bind Maggie — to keep her inside a family structure that consistently diminishes her.
Look at what Eliot does with Tom.
The narrator is extraordinarily clinical — and damning — about the kind of mind Tom represents.

"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye — however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas."
The void of spontaneous ideas — that is a devastating phrase for a man who believes himself to be acting on principle.
Tom is not wicked — he is something more insidious: he is a man who has filled himself with inherited grievance and mistaken it for conscience.
And it is against that wall of inherited righteousness that Maggie's hunger breaks.
I won't entirely defend Tom — Eliot's portrait is too precise for that.
But I want to note what Tom and Maggie share in that terrible moment when ruin first falls on the family.
The passage is one of the most quietly devastating in the novel.
"He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank — as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path."
Tom cannot weep.
Not because he does not feel — but because his nature will not permit the release that Maggie's always seeks.
There is tragedy in Tom too — a smaller tragedy, less interesting, but real.
A black curtain of cloud — suddenly fallen.
That image stays with you because it is so precisely right for Tom — darkness not descending gradually but simply appearing, final, opaque.
And then there is the father.
Seven words — that's all Eliot gives him in one of these passages — but they carry the full weight of a life.
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
That dialect — ay, wench, o'er — it's the voice of a man who has no other language for what he is trying to say.
And what he is trying to say is: I am finished.
What this sequence makes clear — I think all three of you have been circling it — is that Maggie's character is not simply formed by suffering.
It is formed by the collision between the depth of her feeling and the inadequacy of everything around her to receive it.
In our next segment, we'll ask what happens when that collision reaches its most adult and most dangerous form — and what the novel ultimately makes of Maggie's hunger.

segments.title: The Inevitable Current: Fate, Choice, and the Mill's Waters

utterances.text: We've arrived at the final current of our journey today — and it feels right to end where the novel itself begins and ends: with the Mill, with memory, and with the question of whether any of us truly choose our path.
George Eliot opens this novel with one of the most audacious narrative moves in Victorian fiction — a narrator who wakes from a dream and admits the whole opening was a reverie.
And she closes it with a flood that feels both shockingly sudden and utterly inevitable — as if the river was always going to reclaim what belonged to it.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — let's talk about fate, about what is chosen and what is given, and about what this novel finally says about the current we're all caught in.
The opening gambit of this novel is, I think, one of the great sleights of hand in all of English fiction.
Eliot gives us this extraordinary, immersive description of the Mill, the river, the snow — and then she pulls the rug entirely.
She says, in effect — and I love reading this aloud —

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
She's been sitting in a chair the entire time — elbows pressed on the armrests, nodding off — and we were inside her dream.
The entire world of the novel is memory before a single character has spoken a word.
And that framing tells us something absolutely essential about what Eliot is attempting — which is not prophecy, not social tract, but elegy.
The novel is written in full knowledge of how it ends — the flood, the death, the reconciliation that comes too late.
Everything is already lost when the narrator dozes in her chair, and what she dreams back into being is therefore suffused with a grief we cannot yet name.
This connects, I think, to a passage I find almost unbearably moving — Eliot's meditation on what home actually means, and why we cannot choose to stop loving it.
She writes, and I ask you to attend carefully to the rhythm of this —

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
"The labour of choice" — that is the whole novel in three words.
Maggie's tragedy is precisely that she was born into a world that demanded she make choices her nature was never equipped to make in cold blood.
Edmund is right that the phrase lands like a verdict — but I want to push on who bears that labour and who is spared it.
The passage is ostensibly about Tom returning home from school — his happiness, his warmth, his belonging.

But Eliot embeds within it this devastating aside about upholstery and improvement — the striving after something better that she says distinguishes, with exquisite irony, quote, "the British man from the foreign brute."

The joke is sharp enough to cut — because the entire world of the Tullivers is being swept away precisely by that improvement, by creditors and lawyers and market forces that have no affection for old inferior things.

So when she writes that affections have "a trick of twining round those old inferior things" — that our loves have "deep immovable roots in memory" — she is also showing us exactly what capitalism destroys first.
It doesn't just take the mill — it takes the meaning of the mill.
And Eliot makes that devastation human — not abstract — through Mr. Tulliver himself, who is both the victim of those forces and, in his own stubborn way, their instrument.
There is a moment — and it is one of the small great moments of this novel — where Tulliver rides away from a farm, having made some determination, full of resolution.
And then something stops him — some thought — and he reins in his horse and sits there, turning his head from side to side in what the narrator calls "a melancholy way."
And then he speaks aloud — to no one, to the lane, to the cold air —
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
Every time I read that line aloud I have to pause.
Because it is this gruff, limited man — who will never fully understand his daughter — glimpsing with perfect clarity exactly the tragedy that awaits her.
He knows. And he rides back. And there is nothing he can do.
That is Eliot at her most Shakespearean — the inarticulate man who contains, for one unguarded moment, an understanding he can neither express nor act upon.
And the narrator has already told us what this is — that Mr. Tulliver was relapsing into the sense, as she puts it, that "this is a puzzling world."
That phrase — "a puzzling world" — is the most honest thing in the novel.
Not tragic, not comic — puzzling. The right word for a life that refuses the consolations of either genre.
And notice the structure of that moment: he gets outside the yard gate — he is resolute — and it is only in the lane, out of sight of the farm-buildings, that the feeling breaks through.
He cannot afford to feel it in the presence of others. Vulnerability is a private luxury in Tulliver's world.
And what he fears for Maggie is exactly what the novel delivers: dependence on Tom, on the goodwill of a man who loves her but cannot comprehend her.
That is not fate in any mystical sense — that is the structure of a society that gave women no other options.
The river doesn't kill Maggie. The river merely ends what the world had already foreclosed.
That image — the river that ends what the world has already foreclosed — feels like the right place to let the waters carry us for a moment.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — this has been, genuinely, one of the great pleasures of the series.
A novel that begins with a narrator nodding off in a chair, dreaming of a mill she has already lost — and ends in flood and silence and that terrible reunion.
What George Eliot understood — and what I think this conversation has shown — is that we are all, in some sense, pressing our elbows on the arms of the chair.
Dreaming back toward something we can name but cannot hold.
Thank you for joining us for The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c8:p6.text:
For Mr Tulliver was in a position neither new nor striking, but, like other
everyday things, sure to have a cumulative effect that will be felt in the
long run: he was held to be a much more substantial man than he really was. And
as we are all apt to believe what the world believes about us, it was his habit
to think of failure and ruin with the same sort of remote pity with which a
spare, long-necked man hears that his plethoric short-necked neighbour is
stricken with apoplexy. He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about
his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of
land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of
considerable substance. They gave a pleasant flavour to his glass on a
market-day, and if it had not been for the recurrence of half-yearly payments,
Mr Tulliver would really have forgotten that there was a mortgage of two
thousand pounds on his very desirable freehold. That was not altogether his own
fault, since one of the thousand pounds was his sister’s fortune, which
he had to pay on her marriage; and a man who has neighbours that  will  go
to law with him is not likely to pay off his mortgages, especially if he enjoys
the good opinion of acquaintances who want to borrow a hundred pounds on
security too lofty to be represented by parchment. Our friend Mr Tulliver had
a good-natured fibre in him, and did not like to give harsh refusals even to
his sister, who had not only come in to the world in that superfluous way
characteristic of sisters, creating a necessity for mortgages, but had quite
thrown herself away in marriage, and had crowned her mistakes by having an
eighth baby. On this point Mr Tulliver was conscious of being a little weak;
but he apologised to himself by saying that poor Gritty had been a good-looking
wench before she married Moss; he would sometimes say this even with a slight
tremulousness in his voice. But this morning he was in a mood more becoming a
man of business, and in the course of his ride along the Basset lanes, with
their deep ruts,—lying so far away from a market-town that the labour of
drawing produce and manure was enough to take away the best part of the profits
on such poor land as that parish was made of,—he got up a due amount of
irritation against Moss as a man without capital, who, if murrain and blight
were abroad, was sure to have his share of them, and who, the more you tried to
help him out of the mud, would sink the further in. It would do him good rather
than harm, now, if he were obliged to raise this three hundred pounds; it would
make him look about him better, and not act so foolishly about his wool this
year as he did the last; in fact, Mr Tulliver had been too easy with his
brother-in-law, and because he had let the interest run on for two years, Moss
was likely enough to think that he should never be troubled about the
principal. But Mr Tulliver was determined not to encourage such shuffling
people any longer; and a ride along the Basset lanes was not likely to enervate
a man’s resolution by softening his temper. The deep-trodden hoof-marks,
made in the muddiest days of winter, gave him a shake now and then which
suggested a rash but stimulating snarl at the father of lawyers, who, whether
by means of his hoof or otherwise, had doubtless something to do with this
state of the roads; and the abundance of foul land and neglected fences that
met his eye, though they made no part of his brother Moss’s farm,
strongly contributed to his dissatisfaction with that unlucky agriculturist. If
this wasn’t Moss’s fallow, it might have been; Basset was all
alike; it was a beggarly parish, in Mr Tulliver’s opinion, and his
opinion was certainly not groundless. Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a
poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than
half a curate, also poor. If any one strongly impressed with the power of the
human mind to triumph over circumstances will contend that the parishioners of
Basset might nevertheless have been a very superior class of people, I have
nothing to urge against that abstract proposition; I only know that, in point
of fact, the Basset mind was in strict keeping with its circumstances. The
muddy lanes, green or clayey, that seemed to the unaccustomed eye to lead
nowhere but into each other, did really lead, with patience, to a distant
high-road; but there were many feet in Basset which they led more frequently to
a centre of dissipation, spoken of formerly as the “Markis o’
Granby,” but among intimates as “Dickison’s.” A large
low room with a sanded floor; a cold scent of tobacco, modified by undetected
beer-dregs; Mr Dickison leaning against the door-post with a melancholy
pimpled face, looking as irrelevant to the daylight as a last night’s
guttered candle,—all this may not seem a very seductive form of
temptation; but the majority of men in Basset found it fatally alluring when
encountered on their road toward four o’clock on a wintry afternoon; and
if any wife in Basset wished to indicate that her husband was not a
pleasure-seeking man, she could hardly do it more emphatically than by saying
that he didn’t spend a shilling at Dickison’s from one Whitsuntide
to another. Mrs Moss had said so of  her  husband more than once, when
her brother was in a mood to find fault with him, as he certainly was to-day.
And nothing could be less pacifying to Mr Tulliver than the behaviour of the
farmyard gate, which he no sooner attempted to push open with his riding-stick
than it acted as gates without the upper hinge are known to do, to the peril of
shins, whether equine or human. He was about to get down and lead his horse
through the damp dirt of the hollow farmyard, shadowed drearily by the large
half-timbered buildings, up to the long line of tumble-down dwelling-houses
standing on a raised causeway; but the timely appearance of a cowboy saved him
that frustration of a plan he had determined on,—namely, not to get down
from his horse during this visit. If a man means to be hard, let him keep in
his saddle and speak from that height, above the level of pleading eyes, and
with the command of a distant horizon. Mrs Moss heard the sound of the
horse’s feet, and, when her brother rode up, was already outside the
kitchen door, with a half-weary smile on her face, and a black-eyed baby in her
arms. Mrs Moss’s face bore a faded resemblance to her brother’s;
baby’s little fat hand, pressed against her cheek, seemed to show more
strikingly that the cheek was faded.
c8:p6.summary: The narrator exposes Mr Tulliver's false sense of security despite carrying a two-thousand-pound mortgage, his unconscious blindness to his sister's suffering, and his weakness in lending to Moss; the passage then provides a scathing sociological portrait of Basset parish, its poor soil, poverty, and the temptations of Dickison's public house.

Mrs Glegg being in this state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity, I
leave you to judge what effect was produced on her by the reception of a short
letter from Mr Tulliver that very evening, after Mrs Pullet’s
departure, informing her that she needn’t trouble her mind about her five
hundred pounds, for it should be paid back to her in the course of the next
month at farthest, together with the interest due thereon until the time of
payment. And furthermore, that Mr Tulliver had no wish to behave uncivilly to
Mrs Glegg, and she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he
desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
c13:p5.summary: Mr Tulliver writes to Mrs Glegg announcing he will repay her five hundred pounds within a month and neither desires nor requires her favours, completely inverting her anticipated reconciliation.
c13:p5.best_quote: she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
